Peace to you, night-walker, though your words bring a riddle to my resting head. 

We know of no people called Wewush, nor have my hunters or scouts ever laid eyes on their hearth-smoke. Our grain bins are full, by the favor of the earth and the toil of our hands, and we would not grudge a loaf to a starving stranger at our gate—yet I cannot send my people out into the wild to feed a ghost. 

Tell me, spirit, where do these folk dwell? In what direction must a man walk, and for how many suns, before he smells their fires? Bring me a true path to walk, and then we shall speak of grain.

The earth and the sea have been kind to Joawethom. Our granary is heavy with grain, our children smile, and our hearths burn warm, so I do not come begging. It is wood and good stone. Our limbs are many, our roofs are thin hide against the ocean winds, and the trees do not grow as fast as our children. Wind is just air that cannot sit still, spirit. It cools our backs when we sweat, and it rattles the hides when a storm gathers, but it fills no bellies. I know my people, I know our grain keeps us fed, and I know stone and wood do what hands tell them to do. If you have come only to boast of being a breeze, blow along; we have work when the sun rises. But if your wandering has shown you something real—tell me, what lies across the salty water to the northwest, and what shape of fire turns the northern river mud into a pot that will hold broth without crumbling? Speak plainly of earth and water, or leave me to my rest.

Tell me where their path lies upon the earth, or leave me to my rest; a chief cannot load carts for a name that lives only in sleep.
